name: Cottage
tagline: Built by hand, with friends, in the hills
story:
I met Sem and Dafne while volunteering in Hampi. Back story is important — I learned through them how to do what we love and travel, build, and live in tune with nature and our emotions. We were building a small stone pond to chill in the summer. We cooked. We swam in the Bhadra. Explored around. All without any alcohol, no substances — just learned to live peacefully by working and cooking our food. Learning from Dafne: all the music and language and Italian cuisine. Learning from Sem: all the stone building and philosophy.

They visited me after their trip to Rishikesh — they came to Chikmaglur. We wanted to build something together. After our humble new year we started building the wooden cottage. We put stones as foundation in two-foot-deep holes and on that, wood frames — ten by ten, which is not exactly ten by ten, maybe ten by eleven :-)

In ten days we had a floor and four pillars for the roof. Then after they left, I struggled with inspiration, and working alone can be daunting. Somehow, before rain, I got the roof on with help from my dad and his people.

Roof and a floor. Built the wooden walls and fixed some old windows. Got so difficult to move wood during rains because vehicles wouldn't go there — had to carry everything. Carried two heavy generators because there's no power to use power tools. With all this it's reached some shape. But it yet to be finished.
closing: What this made possible was a quiet place to think — a room built with people I'll never forget, in a landscape that shaped how I understand shelter.

name: Watercolors
story:
I've been painting with watercolors since I was a kid, though I only started taking it seriously a few years ago. There's something fundamentally different about painting light onto paper versus mixing pixels on a screen — the way the pigment moves without your permission, the way mistakes are permanent, the way you learn to let go.

These aren't all good. Most of them aren't. But I keep them anyway, because each one is a record of a specific afternoon I can't get back.
closing: What this made possible was a better eye for color, composition, and the fact that not everything needs to be perfect to be worth keeping.

name: ESP32
tagline: Small machines that sense and respond
story:
I got obsessed with the ESP32 after realizing I could connect the physical world to the internet for less than the price of a burrito. Since then I've built a handful of small devices: a soil moisture sensor for my plants, a door sensor that texts me when the mail arrives, a temperature logger with a little e-ink display.

The appeal isn't the connectivity — it's the constraints. Five hundred kilobytes of memory. No operating system. Every byte deliberate. It reminds me why I love embedded systems.
closing: What this made possible was a home that pays attention, and a reminder that the best engineers solve problems they actually have.

name: LUMINARA
story:
LUMINARA is a first-person exploration game I built in C++ using a custom renderer — no Unreal, no Unity, just OpenGL and about eighteen months of evenings. The world is small and quiet: a single floating island with ruins, overgrown gardens, and light that behaves the way you want light to behave rather than the way it actually does.

Building a renderer from scratch will teach you every layer of the graphics stack. But what I really wanted to understand was why certain spaces feel meaningful. The project became a question I kept asking: what makes a place worth being in?
closing: What this made possible was a deep understanding of how GPUs actually work, and a small world that feels like the right size.

name: Workaway
story:
For about two years I traveled while working remotely, staying anywhere from a week to a month — friends' spare rooms, month-long sublets, one genuinely haunted Airbnb. The point wasn't the places; it was the texture of what working somewhere different actually does to your brain.

The best discovery: your environment shapes your creativity more than you think. A change of walls doesn't fix writer's block, but it does make you feel like a different person, and that helps.
closing: What this made possible was a much better understanding of where I do my best work, and the luxury of knowing I can set up anywhere.
